title: What Does a Positive Stain Measure? From Fixed Tissue to Living Cell Biology: Lessons from the Stomach
content: Immunohistochemistry preserves the spatial relationship between molecular signals and tissue architecture, but its biological interpretation is less straightforward than its visual appearance suggests. Antibody binding in a fixed section establishes neither the accessibility of an epitope in living tissue nor the functional activity of the recognised protein. Membrane localisation, nuclear retention, staining intensity and cellular distribution are distinct measurements, each supporting different conclusions. Gastric adenocarcinoma provides an informative example because several clinically validated assays interrogate these properties within the same specimen. This critical narrative review examines the effects of fixation and antigen retrieval, membrane organisation and protein trafficking, cellular attribution, quantitative signal generation and spatial sampling on the interpretation of immunohistochemical findings. Building on established methodological literature, it proposes a measurement-to-claim framework that identifies the evidentiary gap between a histochemical observation and the biological conclusion drawn from it. The framework is intended neither as a new diagnostic score nor as an alternative to validated clinical thresholds. Its proposed contribution is to match specific interpretative uncertainties to complementary methods capable of addressing them. Applications extend beyond gastric pathology to receptor biology, developmental histology, neuroscience and quantitative tissue imaging. Its practical value remains to be tested experimentally. The central argument is that a reproducible stain becomes biologically informative only when the conclusion attributed to it is proportionate to the measurement performed.
